item.text: The active selected scope is `1B` only (`selected_theme_ids: ["1B"]`), so I’m treating the other chapter reviews as queued rather than silently expanding this continuation. I’ve now recovered target-period cyber policy/response records, a direct Trọng military-authority record, nuclear-safety governance and facility status, AI-readiness context, biosafety capacity context, and contrary cyber-attribution/censorship evidence.

Filesystem access remained read-only, so I could not persist changes to `research-ledger-manifest.json`. The following is the permissive handoff for the active selected scope, Chapter `1B`; IDs continue from `E027`.

### New retained evidence

- **E028 — 2022 national cybersecurity strategy.**  
  On 11 August 2022, Vietnam’s Government issued a strategy through 2025/2030 emphasizing Party leadership, state management, protection of critical digital infrastructure, and cyber sovereignty. Official policy record; indirect attribution to Trọng through party authority, not proof of personal authorship. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.9`, `1B.10`. [Vietnam Government Portal, lines 154–183](https://en.baochinhphu.vn/govt-issues-national-strategy-to-combat-new-cyber-security-challenges-111220811103436282.htm)

- **E029 — Cyber incident-response architecture.**  
  The strategy required incident-response teams across eleven priority sectors, including transport, energy, health, finance, defense, security, and government administration. This is a formal shielding and preparedness measure; implementation was not independently verified. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.10`. [Vietnam Government Portal, lines 192–197](https://en.baochinhphu.vn/govt-issues-national-strategy-to-combat-new-cyber-security-challenges-111220811103436282.htm)

- **E030 — Official acknowledgment of cyber-risk exposure.**  
  The October 2022 cyber directive stated that cyber incidents could cause serious damage and that Vietnam’s existing response was not yet sufficiently proactive or timely. This is adverse evidence against treating the strategy as proof of effective protection. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.9`, `1B.10`. [Vietnam Ministry of Science and Technology, lines 79–90](https://english.mst.gov.vn/vietnam-steps-up-response-to-cyberinformation-security-incidents-197155394.htm)

- **E031 — Corrective cyber-response directive.**  
  Directive 18/CT-TTg required vulnerability scans at least every six months, response plans by 31 December 2022, annual exercises for higher-risk systems, remediation of weaknesses, and expanded incident-response teams. This is the clearest target-period corrective-action record, although it was issued by Prime Minister Phạm Minh Chính rather than Trọng. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.9`, `1B.10`. [Vietnam Government Portal, lines 154–177](https://en.baochinhphu.vn/prime-minister-orders-strengthening-response-to-cyberinformation-security-incidents-111221014153312753.htm)

- **E032 — Trọng’s formal military-security authority.**  
  On 19–20 December 2022, Nguyễn Phú Trọng chaired or directed the Central Military Commission and attended the national military-political conference as its secretary. This establishes formal authority over the party’s military-security apparatus during the target period, not a specific cyber or catastrophic-risk order. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.10`. [Vietnam News, 19 December 2022](https://vietnamnews.vn/politics-laws/1437875/central-military-commission-told-to-maintain-combat-readiness-and-strengthen-capacity.html); [Vietnam Government Portal, lines 179–189](https://baochinhphu.vn/hoi-nghi-quan-chinh-toan-quan-danh-gia-ket-qua-cong-tac-quan-su-quoc-phong-nam-2022-102221220113845866.htm)

- **E033 — Military management of cyberspace.**  
  The 20 December conference record states that Vietnam’s armed forces maintained readiness, managed airspace, maritime space, borders, internal territory, and cyberspace, and reviewed operational documents. The report is official and outcome-heavy; it does not specify Trọng’s individual instruction or implementation verification. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.10`. [Vietnam Government Portal, lines 205–211](https://baochinhphu.vn/hoi-nghi-quan-chinh-toan-quan-danh-gia-ket-qua-cong-tac-quan-su-quoc-phong-nam-2022-102221220113845866.htm)

- **E034 — Non-traditional security preparedness.**  
  Contemporary reporting on Trọng’s Central Military Commission meeting says he ordered readiness and preparation for non-traditional security challenges. Attribution is direct for the general instruction, but the record does not identify biological, AI, nuclear-command, or cyber-operation details. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.10`. [Vietnam News](https://vietnamnews.vn/politics-laws/1437875/central-military-commission-told-to-maintain-combat-readiness-and-strengthen-capacity.html)

- **E035 — Vietnam had no nuclear power installation in 2022.**  
  Vietnam’s national report to the IAEA stated that the country had no nuclear installation, while operating the 500 kW Da Lat research reactor. This materially limits the catastrophic-exposure baseline but does not establish Trọng’s personal conduct. Maps `1B.1`, `1B.3`, `1B.4`, `1B.5`. [IAEA national report, pp. 60–61 / lines 1890–1906](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/23/11/vietnam_cns_national_report_8-9th_rm_in_2023.pdf)

- **E036 — Nuclear-safety governance allocation.**  
  The IAEA report describes government-wide atomic-energy responsibility, VARANS safety assessment, ministerial licensing roles, and a National Nuclear Safety Council advising on safety and serious incidents. This supports institutional shielding and command-safety context, but the framework predates 2022 and is not Trọng-specific. Maps `1B.3`, `1B.5`, `1B.10`. [IAEA national report, pp. 17–20 / lines 533–556, 614–618](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/23/11/vietnam_cns_national_report_8-9th_rm_in_2023.pdf)

- **E037 — Research-reactor safety and security controls.**  
  The IAEA report records HEU-to-LEU conversion, instrumentation and control upgrades, safety-analysis review, inspections, and monitoring of the Da Lat reactor’s aging issues. These are positive institutional safety measures, not evidence of Trọng’s personal decision. Maps `1B.3`, `1B.5`, `1B.10`. [IAEA national report, pp. 60–61 / lines 1894–1903](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/23/11/vietnam_cns_national_report_8-9th_rm_in_2023.pdf)

- **E038 — 2022 biosafety capacity.**  
  JICA reported inauguration of a Biosafety Level-3 laboratory in January 2022 and described Vietnam’s capacity to handle high-risk pathogens. This is useful favorable biological-security context, but it is a donor/project record rather than evidence of Trọng’s direction or oversight. Maps `1B.5`, `1B.6`, `1B.10`. [JICA project record](https://www.jica.go.jp/english/overseas/vietnam/information/press/2021/__icsFiles/afieldfile/2024/09/10/press220117_en.pdf)

- **E039 — AI governance/readiness context.**  
  Oxford Insights’ 2022 Government AI Readiness Index placed Vietnam 55th globally and 6th in ASEAN, with assessment dimensions including data, technical capacity, adaptability, governance, ethics, and vision. This indicates moderate institutional readiness, not catastrophic-risk governance or Trọng attribution. Maps `1B.6`, `1B.9`, `1B.10`. [Vietnam Government Portal, lines 181–195](https://baochinhphu.vn/viet-nam-tang-7-bac-ve-chi-so-san-sang-tri-tue-nhan-tao-toan-cau-2022-102221228191945001.htm)

- **E040 — Cyber-censorship and suspension powers.**  
  Freedom House reported that Decree 53/2022, effective October 2022, empowered security authorities to order removals, suspend information systems, and revoke domain names on national-security or cybersecurity grounds. This is adverse dual-use and information-control evidence, not catastrophic cyber misuse. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.9`. [Freedom House, lines 183–187](https://freedomhouse.org/country/vietnam/freedom-net/2022)

- **E041 — Cyber-espionage capability and attribution risk.**  
  Freedom House cited FireEye’s assessment that Vietnam had developed significant cyber-espionage capabilities and tracked Ocean Lotus/APT32 attacks. This is external adverse context, but it does not establish a 2022 operation, official authorization, or Trọng’s knowledge. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.9`. [Freedom House, lines 337–339](https://freedomhouse.org/country/vietnam/freedom-net/2022)

- **E042 — Contrary attribution limitation.**  
  A Cyber Defense Review analysis noted that APT32/Ocean Lotus was linked to Vietnam by private cybersecurity firms, while explicitly stating that this was not demonstrably official Vietnamese government action. This should constrain attribution rather than be counted as proof of state or ruler conduct. Maps `1B.7`, `1B.9`. [Cyber Defense Review, pp. 97–98 / lines 2388–2411](https://cyberdefensereview.army.mil/Portals/6/Documents/2022_winter/CDR_V7N1_WINTER_2022_Special_Edition_r7.pdf)

### Search and disposition notes

Targeted English and Vietnamese searches were attempted for:

- Trọng plus nuclear weapons, nuclear safety, NPT, biological security, biosafety, AI, cyber operations, command authority, and crisis response.
- Favorable and adverse cyber-policy and incident-response terms.
- Contrary searches for state-linked cyber operations, nuclear incidents, biological incidents, and AI-risk governance.

No traceable 2022 personal statement, order, appointment, nuclear/biological/AI incident, cyber operation, command-safety failure, or corrective investigation attributable specifically to Trọng was recovered.

Recommended manifest dispositions:

- Retain `E028–E042` as `retained`, with the methodology mappings above.
- Reclassify `E026` and `E027` as overlapping adverse cyber-control context; do not count them as independent catastrophic-risk corroboration.
- Retain `E022` and `E024` as `gateway_only`.
- Retain `E025` and `E038` as `context` unless the ledger permits institutional-capacity evidence under `1B.5`/`1B.6`.
- Record the absence of Trọng-specific catastrophic-risk decisions as a `research_gap`, never as negative ruler evidence.

No score, score range, ranking recommendation, or null recommendation was assigned.
